Hosea 1.audience: Hosea prophesied to the northern kingdom of Israel in the days of Jeroboam II and the kings of Judah from Uzziah to Hezekiah (Hosea 1:1), about 755–715 BC—Israel's last decades before Assyria destroyed it in 722 BC.

culture.title: Children's names as messages
culture.text: Jezreel recalls Jehu's bloodshed at the city of Jezreel (2 Kings 10:11); Loruhamah means ‘not pitied’ and Loammi ‘not my people.’

culture.title: Jeroboam II
culture.text: Jeroboam II ruled forty-one years and restored Israel's borders (2 Kings 14:23–25). It was a time of wealth before a rapid collapse.

Hosea 2.audience: Israel had credited its grain, wine, oil, wool, and flax to Baal (Hosea 2:5, 8). Hosea's hearers lived in a farming society that depended on rain.

culture.title: Baal as giver of crops
culture.text: Canaanites worshipped Baal as the storm god who sent rain and fertility. Israel offered him the very silver and gold God had given.

culture.title: Ishi and Baali
culture.text: Both words mean ‘my husband’; "Baali" also means ‘my Baal.’ God will no longer be called by the name of Baal.

culture.title: The valley of Achor
culture.text: Achor was where Achan was judged at the conquest (Joshua 7:24–26). It will become "a door of hope."

Hosea 3.audience: Hosea buys back his unfaithful wife as a sign of God's love for Israel, which will live "many days without a king" (Hosea 3:4).

culture.title: Silver and barley
culture.text: Hosea pays fifteen pieces of silver and a homer and a half of barley—payment partly in silver and partly in grain.

culture.title: Ephod and teraphim
culture.text: The ephod was used to seek God's answers; teraphim were household idols. Israel will be without both legitimate and illegitimate means of worship.

Hosea 4.audience: God brings a charge against the people and priests of Israel: "there is no truth, nor mercy, nor knowledge of God in the land" (Hosea 4:1).

culture.title: Bethaven
culture.text: Hosea calls Bethel (‘house of God’) Bethaven (‘house of wickedness’) because of the golden calf there (1 Kings 12:29).

culture.title: Asking counsel of a stick
culture.text: "My people ask counsel at their stocks, and their staff declareth unto them"—divination using wooden objects or rods.

culture.title: Shrines under trees
culture.text: Sacrifices were offered on hilltops under oaks, poplars, and elms "because the shadow thereof is good."

Hosea 5.audience: Hosea addresses priests, Israel, and the king's house, warning of judgment on Ephraim and Judah. Ephraim had turned to the king of Assyria for help (Hosea 5:13).

culture.title: Alarm at Gibeah and Ramah
culture.text: Gibeah, Ramah, and Bethaven were towns on the border of Benjamin, where invasion would be announced by trumpet.

culture.title: Moving boundaries
culture.text: Judah's princes are like those who remove boundary stones (Deuteronomy 19:14).

Hosea 6.audience: Israel's repentance is "as a morning cloud" (Hosea 6:4). Jesus twice quoted verse 6, "I desired mercy, and not sacrifice" (Matthew 9:13; 12:7).

culture.title: Morning dew
culture.text: Summer dew in Israel is heavy at dawn and vanishes as soon as the sun rises.

culture.title: Rain in its season
culture.text: The "latter and former rain" came in spring and autumn, essential for crops.

Hosea 7.audience: Hosea describes palace intrigue and alliances with Egypt and Assyria. Four of Israel's last six kings were assassinated (2 Kings 15).

culture.title: A baker's oven
culture.text: Conspirators are like an oven left heating through the night—the fire smoldering until it flares up and consumes their judges and kings.

culture.title: A silly dove
culture.text: Ephraim flutters between Egypt and Assyria. King Hoshea paid tribute to Assyria and then sought help from Egypt (2 Kings 17:3–4).

culture.title: A cake not turned
culture.text: Flat bread baked on hot stones had to be turned; otherwise it burned on one side and stayed raw on the other.

Hosea 8.audience: Hosea condemns Israel's kings, idols, and foreign alliances: "they have sown the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind" (Hosea 8:7).

culture.title: The calf of Samaria
culture.text: The golden calves at Bethel and Dan were the official worship of the northern kingdom.

culture.title: Hiring lovers
culture.text: Ephraim "hath hired lovers"—paying tribute to Assyria, as Menahem did (2 Kings 15:19–20).

Hosea 9.audience: Hosea warns that Israel will not stay in the LORD's land but will eat unclean food in Assyria and return to "Egypt" (Hosea 9:3).

culture.title: Harvest festivals
culture.text: Grain floors and winepresses were places of celebration at harvest, and of Baal worship.

culture.title: Memphis shall bury them
culture.text: Memphis (Moph) had vast cemeteries; refugees to Egypt would die there.

culture.title: The days of Gibeah
culture.text: Gibeah recalls the crime and civil war of Judges 19–21.

Hosea 10.audience: Israel is a luxuriant vine that multiplied altars. Its people will say to the mountains, "Cover us" (Hosea 10:8), words Jesus spoke on the way to the cross (Luke 23:30).

culture.title: Betharbel
culture.text: "As Shalman spoiled Betharbel"—a brutal attack remembered by Hosea's hearers, though the event is not otherwise recorded.

culture.title: A heifer threshing
culture.text: A heifer treading out grain could eat as it worked (Deuteronomy 25:4); plowing under a yoke was harder labor.

Hosea 11.audience: God speaks of Israel as a son he loved and called out of Egypt (Hosea 11:1), a verse Matthew applies to Jesus' return from Egypt (Matthew 2:15).

culture.title: Teaching a child to walk
culture.text: "I taught Ephraim also to go, taking them by their arms"—a parent holding a toddler's arms.

culture.title: Admah and Zeboim
culture.text: Admah and Zeboim were destroyed with Sodom and Gomorrah (Deuteronomy 29:23).

Hosea 12.audience: Hosea recalls Jacob's struggles—taking his brother by the heel, wrestling with the angel, and meeting God at Bethel (Hosea 12:3–4).

culture.title: Deceitful balances
culture.text: The word for "merchant" is "Canaan"—the Canaanites were known as traders. Dishonest weights cheated buyers.

culture.title: Oil carried to Egypt
culture.text: Israel made a covenant with Assyria and sent olive oil to Egypt as a gift—playing both sides.

Hosea 13.audience: Hosea announces Ephraim's death. Paul quotes verse 14 in 1 Corinthians 15:55: "O death, where is thy sting?"

culture.title: Kissing the calves
culture.text: Worshippers kissed idols as an act of devotion (1 Kings 19:18).

culture.title: Morning cloud and chaff
culture.text: Ephraim will vanish like morning mist, dew, chaff blown from the threshing floor, and smoke from a chimney.

culture.title: The east wind
culture.text: The hot east wind from the desert dried up springs and withered crops.

Hosea 14.audience: The book ends with a call to return and words to say, and with promises of healing for Israel.

culture.title: The calves of our lips
culture.text: Israel offers words of repentance and praise in place of bull sacrifices (compare Hebrews 13:15).

culture.title: Lebanon's cedars and wine
culture.text: Lebanon was famous for cedars, fragrance, and wine—pictures of restored beauty.

Joel 1.audience: Joel son of Pethuel addresses elders, drunkards, farmers, and priests during a locust plague and drought (Joel 1:2–13). The book gives no date.

culture.title: Four kinds of locust
culture.text: The palmerworm, locust, cankerworm, and caterpillar may be stages in a locust's growth or different kinds. Swarms can strip every green plant from a region.

culture.title: Offerings cut off
culture.text: Without grain and grapes, the daily meat offering and drink offering at the temple could not be made.

culture.title: Barked fig trees
culture.text: Locusts eat the bark of vines and fig trees, leaving the branches white.

Joel 2.audience: Joel calls Judah to repent: "rend your heart, and not your garments" (Joel 2:13). Peter quoted verses 28–32 at Pentecost (Acts 2:16–21).

culture.title: A locust army
culture.text: Locusts advance like horses and chariots, climbing walls and entering windows. Locust heads resemble small horses' heads.

culture.title: A solemn assembly
culture.text: A trumpet called everyone—elders, children, nursing infants, even newlyweds—to a fast at the temple.

culture.title: The northern army
culture.text: The locusts are driven into the desert, the Dead Sea ("east sea"), and the Mediterranean ("utmost sea").

Joel 3.audience: Joel speaks of the nations gathered for judgment in the valley of Jehoshaphat and accuses Tyre, Sidon, and Philistia of selling Judeans to the Greeks (Joel 3:4–6).

culture.title: Plowshares into swords
culture.text: Joel reverses Isaiah's image (Isaiah 2:4): the nations prepare for war.

culture.title: Slave trading
culture.text: Phoenician merchants traded slaves across the Mediterranean, including to the Grecians (Javan).

culture.title: The valley of Jehoshaphat
culture.text: Jehoshaphat means ‘the LORD judges.’ Tradition later identified the valley with the Kidron valley outside Jerusalem.

Amos 1.audience: Amos, a herdman from Tekoa in Judah, preached to the northern kingdom "two years before the earthquake" (Amos 1:1), in the days of Uzziah and Jeroboam II, about 760 BC.

culture.title: The earthquake
culture.text: A great earthquake in Uzziah's reign was remembered centuries later (Zechariah 14:5). Excavations at Hazor and other sites show earthquake damage from this period.

culture.title: Three transgressions and four
culture.text: Each oracle begins "For three transgressions... and for four"—a number pattern from wisdom sayings meaning sin piled on sin.

culture.title: Threshing sledges of iron
culture.text: Damascus threshed Gilead with iron-studded sledges—a brutal treatment of a conquered people.

Amos 2.audience: After condemning six neighbors, Amos turns to Judah and then to Israel, his real audience.

culture.title: Sold for a pair of shoes
culture.text: The poor were sold into debt slavery for trivial debts—even the price of a pair of sandals.

culture.title: Garments taken in pledge
culture.text: Creditors kept the poor's cloaks overnight—forbidden by the law (Exodus 22:26)—and lay on them beside altars.

culture.title: Burning bones into lime
culture.text: Moab burned the bones of Edom's king to lime—desecrating a royal grave.

Amos 3.audience: Amos speaks to "the whole family which I brought up from the land of Egypt" (Amos 3:1) and to the rich in Samaria.

culture.title: Winter and summer houses
culture.text: The wealthy kept separate winter and summer houses, decorated with ivory. Carved ivory panels from this period have been found at Samaria.

culture.title: Horns of the altar
culture.text: Cutting off the altar's horns at Bethel would remove its sanctity and any place of refuge.

culture.title: Two legs and a piece of an ear
culture.text: A shepherd brought back remains of an animal killed by a lion as proof he had not stolen it (Exodus 22:13).

Amos 4.audience: Amos addresses the wealthy women of Samaria as "kine of Bashan" who oppress the poor (Amos 4:1).

culture.title: Cows of Bashan
culture.text: Bashan's cattle were famous for being well-fed. The wealthy women demand that their husbands bring drink.

culture.title: Tithes every three years
culture.text: Amos mocks worshippers at Bethel and Gilgal for bringing sacrifices and tithes with great show.

Amos 5.audience: Amos laments over Israel and calls, "let judgment run down as waters" (Amos 5:24). Stephen quotes verses 25–27 (Acts 7:42–43).

culture.title: Justice in the gate
culture.text: Elders judged cases in the city gate. The powerful took bribes and turned aside the poor there.

culture.title: Taxing the poor's grain
culture.text: The rich took burdens of wheat from the poor and built houses of hewn stone—costly squared masonry.

culture.title: Star gods
culture.text: Chiun is probably Kaiwan, a Mesopotamian name for the planet Saturn, worshipped as a god.

Amos 6.audience: Amos warns those "at ease in Zion" and secure in Samaria, who feast while ignoring the ruin of Joseph (Amos 6:1, 6).

culture.title: Beds of ivory
culture.text: The rich lounged on ivory-inlaid couches, eating lambs and calves from the stall.

culture.title: Wine in bowls and fine oil
culture.text: They drank from large bowls and anointed themselves with the best oils—luxuries of the elite.

culture.title: The marzeah feast
culture.text: "The banquet of them that stretched themselves" (marzeah) was a feast of the wealthy, known from texts at Ugarit.

Amos 7.audience: Amos sees visions of locusts, fire, and a plumbline. Amaziah, priest of Bethel, tells him to go home to Judah (Amos 7:12–13).

culture.title: A plumbline
culture.text: A weight on a cord showed whether a wall was straight. A crooked wall had to be torn down.

culture.title: The king's sanctuary
culture.text: Bethel was "the king's chapel"—the royal shrine of the northern kingdom.

culture.title: Gatherer of sycomore fruit
culture.text: Sycomore figs had to be pierced or nicked to ripen properly—seasonal work for laborers.

Amos 8.audience: Amos sees a basket of summer fruit and condemns merchants eager for the sabbath to end so they can cheat the poor (Amos 8:4–6).

culture.title: Summer fruit and the end
culture.text: The Hebrew for "summer fruit" (qayits) sounds like "end" (qets)—a wordplay.

culture.title: Small ephah, great shekel
culture.text: Merchants used a small measure to sell grain and a heavy weight to receive silver, and sold the chaff with the wheat.

Amos 9.audience: The book ends with God raising up "the tabernacle of David that is fallen" (Amos 9:11), which James quoted at the Jerusalem council (Acts 15:16–17).

culture.title: Caphtor and Kir
culture.text: God brought the Philistines from Caphtor (Crete) and the Syrians from Kir, as he brought Israel from Egypt.

culture.title: Sifting grain
culture.text: Grain was shaken in a sieve so that stones stayed behind while the grain fell through.

culture.title: The plowman overtaking the reaper
culture.text: Harvests will be so plentiful that plowing for the next season starts before reaping is finished.

Obadiah 1.audience: Obadiah's single chapter is addressed to Edom, which stood by and joined in when Jerusalem was plundered (Obadiah 1:11–14). Obadiah 1:1–6 closely parallels Jeremiah 49:9–16.

culture.title: Dwelling in the clefts of the rock
culture.text: Edom's cities were built among high sandstone cliffs, easy to defend. The later Nabataean city of Petra lies in this region.

culture.title: The wise men of Edom
culture.text: Edom, especially Teman, was known for wisdom (Jeremiah 49:7).

culture.title: Sepharad
culture.text: Sepharad was a place where exiles from Jerusalem lived, possibly Sardis in Asia Minor. In later Jewish usage it came to mean Spain.

Jonah 1.audience: Jonah son of Amittai was a prophet in the days of Jeroboam II (2 Kings 14:25). Israel's hearers knew Nineveh as the capital of Assyria, the empire that later destroyed the northern kingdom.

culture.title: Tarshish
culture.text: Tarshish was a distant port in the far west, often identified with Tartessus in Spain—the opposite direction from Nineveh.

culture.title: Joppa
culture.text: Joppa was the main port on Israel's coast; Peter later received his vision there (Acts 10:5).

culture.title: Sailors' gods and lots
culture.text: Sailors from many lands each cried to their own gods, then cast lots to find who was to blame for the storm.

Jonah 2.audience: Jonah prays from inside the fish, using language found throughout the Psalms (compare Psalm 42:7; 120:1).

culture.title: The depths and the weeds
culture.text: "The weeds were wrapped about my head"—seaweed in the depths, an image of drowning.

culture.title: Looking toward the temple
culture.text: Jonah resolves to look again toward God's holy temple—prayer directed toward the temple (1 Kings 8:38).

Jonah 3.audience: Jonah preaches in Nineveh, "an exceeding great city of three days' journey" (Jonah 3:3), and the whole city repents. Jesus cited the men of Nineveh (Matthew 12:41).

culture.title: Nineveh's size
culture.text: Nineveh's walls ran about seven and a half miles around; with its surrounding district it was a vast city.

culture.title: Sackcloth on animals
culture.text: Even animals were covered with sackcloth. Herodotus describes Persians shearing their horses in mourning.

culture.title: A royal decree
culture.text: The king and his nobles issue the fast together—Assyrian decrees were made by the king with his great men.

Jonah 4.audience: The book ends with God's question to Jonah about pity for Nineveh, with its 120,000 people and much cattle (Jonah 4:11).

culture.title: A booth east of the city
culture.text: Jonah builds a shelter of branches to wait and watch the city—like the booths built in fields.

culture.title: The gourd
culture.text: The plant is often identified with the castor-oil plant, which grows quickly and has large leaves.

culture.title: A vehement east wind
culture.text: The hot east wind (sirocco) can raise temperatures sharply and cause exhaustion.

Micah 1.audience: Micah of Moresheth prophesied in the days of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah (Micah 1:1), about 740–700 BC, concerning both Samaria and Jerusalem.

culture.title: Wordplays on towns
culture.text: Micah plays on the names of Judean towns near his home: "Tell it not in Gath" (sounds like ‘tell’), "in the house of Aphrah roll thyself in the dust" (Aphrah sounds like ‘dust’).

culture.title: Samaria as heaps
culture.text: Samaria will become a heap in the field; it fell to Assyria in 722 BC.

culture.title: Going stripped and naked
culture.text: Micah wails and goes barefoot and stripped in mourning, like Isaiah's sign (Isaiah 20:2–4).

Micah 2.audience: Micah condemns those who lie awake planning to seize fields and houses (Micah 2:1–2).

culture.title: Coveting fields
culture.text: Wealthy landowners seized family land, breaking the law that kept inheritance in each family.

culture.title: A prophet of wine
culture.text: "I will prophesy unto thee of wine and of strong drink"—the kind of prophet the people wanted.

Micah 3.audience: Micah condemns the heads, priests, and prophets of Jerusalem who judge for bribes. Elders in Jeremiah's day quoted verse 12 (Jeremiah 26:18).

culture.title: Zion plowed as a field
culture.text: Jerusalem will be plowed like a field and the temple mount become a wooded hill.

culture.title: Prophets for hire
culture.text: Priests taught for hire and prophets divined for money while claiming the LORD was among them.

Micah 4.audience: Micah 4:1–3 is nearly identical to Isaiah 2:2–4; Micah and Isaiah were contemporaries.

culture.title: Under his vine and fig tree
culture.text: "They shall sit every man under his vine and under his fig tree"—a picture of peace and secure ownership (1 Kings 4:25). George Washington often used the phrase in his letters.

culture.title: Taken to Babylon
culture.text: Micah says Zion will go to Babylon and be rescued there—at a time when Assyria was the great power.

Micah 5.audience: Micah speaks of a ruler from Bethlehem Ephratah (Micah 5:2), quoted by the chief priests to Herod (Matthew 2:5–6).

culture.title: Bethlehem Ephratah
culture.text: Bethlehem was David's hometown (1 Samuel 16:1); Ephratah was the name of its clan or district (Ruth 1:2).

culture.title: Smiting the judge on the cheek
culture.text: Striking a ruler on the cheek was a deep public insult.

culture.title: The land of Nimrod
culture.text: Assyria is called the land of Nimrod (Genesis 10:8–11).

Micah 6.audience: God brings a lawsuit against his people before the mountains and asks what he has done to them. The answer is "to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God" (Micah 6:8).

culture.title: Thousands of rams
culture.text: The worshipper asks whether God wants thousands of rams, rivers of oil, or even a firstborn son—escalating offerings.

culture.title: Wicked balances
culture.text: Merchants used false balances and a bag of deceitful weights.

culture.title: The statutes of Omri
culture.text: Omri and his son Ahab led Israel into Baal worship (1 Kings 16:25–33).

Micah 7.audience: Micah laments a society where "a man's enemies are the men of his own house" (Micah 7:6), echoed by Jesus (Matthew 10:35–36). The book ends with hope in God's mercy.

culture.title: Gleaning after harvest
culture.text: Micah is like someone who comes after the grape and fig harvest and finds no fruit left.

culture.title: Casting sins into the sea
culture.text: "Thou wilt cast all their sins into the depths of the sea." Jewish communities practice a ceremony called Tashlich at the new year, reciting these verses by water.
